analysis.one_liner: Ends tax deductions for junk-food advertising aimed at children.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote and died in the House Ways and Means Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would deny companies a federal tax deduction for marketing to children (age 17 or under) any food or drink that the Treasury Department, working with health officials, deems nutritionally poor. It covers every kind of promotion: TV, radio, print, online and social media ads, product placement in movies and video games, packaging, celebrity endorsements, toys and character tie-ins, and even marketing inside schools. The idea is to raise the cost of advertising sugary and heavily processed food directly to kids, since taxpayers currently subsidize that spending as an ordinary business expense.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and their families benefit if the bill works as intended: with marketing to kids no longer tax-deductible, companies would have less financial backing for the ads, packaging tricks, and in-school promotions that push sugary drinks and processed snacks at children. Taxpayers also benefit slightly, because they stop subsidizing that marketing as a business cost.

how_it_helps.text: Denies a federal tax deduction for any marketing directed at children that promotes food of poor nutritional quality, including related travel, entertainment, gifts, and other promotion expenses.

Covers the full range of techniques used to reach kids: TV, radio, print, social media and internet ads, product placement in movies and video games, packaging and labeling, retail displays, toy and character licensing, celebrity endorsements, and in-school marketing.
Treats marketing as 'directed at' children when at least 35 percent of a media audience is children, so companies cannot narrowly avoid the rule by running broad campaigns on kid-heavy channels.

Leaves the definition of 'food of poor nutritional quality' to the Treasury Department in consultation with HHS and the FTC, keyed to the government's own Dietary Guidelines for Americans, so the standard tracks official nutrition science rather than a fixed list written into law.

analysis.who_pays: Food and beverage companies, fast-food chains, and the advertising and media businesses that sell kid-directed marketing would pay if the bill passed: their marketing to children would no longer be tax-deductible, meaning higher after-tax costs for those campaigns and likely less such marketing overall.

drawbacks.text: The definition of 'food of poor nutritional quality' is left to executive-branch determination by Treasury, HHS, and the FTC, which could invite lobbying over where the line is drawn and make costs less predictable for food companies that also sell nutritious products.

A tax-deduction denial raises the price of advertising rather than banning it, so its real-world effect on what children eat is indirect and uncertain; companies could shift marketing budgets to other forms of promotion.

The 35 percent child-audience threshold and the long list of covered marketing techniques would impose compliance and reporting costs on advertisers and media companies, including ones selling mostly adult programming.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to children runs through a blunt but genuine lever: making kid-directed junk-food marketing a non-deductible expense raises its cost, which is exactly how the tax code shifts business behavior. The main cost is borne by food marketers and ad-supported media, and the rule depends on executive-branch definitions that could be contested. On balance the design is coherent and the burden falls on the industry creating the health problem, but the health benefit is indirect and hard to guarantee.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up, so it died there when the 113th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro introduced the bill on July 25, 2013, joined by Reps. Lee of California, DeFazio, Clay, and Grijalva.
The same day it was introduced, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which holds jurisdiction over tax law.
No further action appears in the legislative record: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action occurred before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.
The bill attracted 26 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no Republicans signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Food and beverage companies, fast-food chains, and ad-supported media are better off, because the marketing they direct at children remains fully tax-deductible. Taxpayers continue to subsidize that spending as an ordinary business cost.

for.name: Barbara Lee

sides.party_line_note: All 26 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republicans signed on, and the Republican-chaired tax committee never moved the bill.

industries.note: These companies' marketing to children would no longer be tax-deductible, raising the after-tax cost of the campaigns that build demand for sugary drinks and processed snacks among kids. Their interest in keeping the deduction runs against children's health, which the bill is meant to serve.

Ad agencies, TV and radio broadcasters, movie and video-game distributors, and mobile app makers sell much of the kid-directed promotion the bill covers; non-deductibility would make that revenue stream more expensive for their clients and likely shrink it.

Chains use toy tie-ins, character licensing, retail displays, and in-school promotions to reach children, all explicitly covered by the bill, and would face higher after-tax costs for those campaigns.
